newsitem.title: MOROCCO: U.N. envoy Baker set to tackle W.Sahara dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy Baker set to tackle W.Sahara dispute.

text.p: U.N. special envoy James Baker is expected in Rabat on Tuesday to tackle a 21-year-old conflict which has defied U.N. peace efforts and kept relations between neighbours Morocco and Algeria cool for years.

A U.N. spokesman said last week Baker, envoy for the disputed Western Sahara, would start his visit to the region on Tuesday. Moroccan officials said he was expected on Tuesday, although a foreign ministry official said he may not arrive until Wednesday.

"The U.N. envoy is expected in Rabat on Tuesday in the day. He will hold talks with interior ministry officials, including (minister) Driss Basri...this is what we know at present," a communications ministry official said on Monday.

Baker, a former U.S. Secretary of State whose diplomacy helped convene the 1991 Madrid peace conference on the Middle East, was appointed last month as personal envoy to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan.

Annan has expressed frustration with the failure to hold a U.N.-brokered referendum, originally planned for January 1992, to decide whether the former Spanish colony should be integrated in Morocco or should be independent.
Morocco claims and largely controls the territory, while the Polisario Front seeks independence for the Sahrawi people.
The referendum has been delayed by disputes over who should be allowed to vote, and U.N. registering of voters collapsed last year.

Fighting in the territory ended in September 1991 with a U.N.-sponsored ceasefire, which has since been monitored by a U.N. force known as Minurso, whose numbers have been reduced to some 230 military obvservers and support personnel.

"At this stage, what we know is that Mr Baker is going to visit Rabat, Tindouf, Algiers and Nouakchott (in neighbouring Mauritania)," a Minurso spokeswoman said in Layoune, the capital of Western Sahara.
Tindouf is a main Polisario camp just inside Algeria which has long backed Polisario's claim for independence.
The Security Council last month expressed disappointed at the lack of progress in organising the referendum and warned that any breach of the ceasefire "could seriously threaten regional stability".
The Polisario, whose leader Mohamed Abdelaziz said last month war could resume if the U.N. plan was not implemented, has welcomed Baker's appointment.
The U.N. said Baker's visit was to "make a fresh assessment of the situation", examine obstacles to implementing the settlement plan, and report back to Annan.
